Passive of Modal Verbs: Ought To
We use the passive voice when we want to emphasize on the action but not on the person who does it. Passive voice can be used anytime with modal verbs. Let's see with Ought to.

Ought to is always used to talk about obligations and duties.

Example
She ought to know what a process in an operating system is.

When we use the passive voice with a modal verb, we simply follow the same structure of the passive and add the verb “be” after the modal verb. See the following structure:

Subject + ought to be + verb in past participle + complement


Examples
The report ought to be finished by next Friday.
This road ought to be repaired. It is impossible for cars to go through.
In a background process, different functions ought to be consolidated, so we don't need many programs to handle each user.
User processes are a little different. Their main function is run software code of an application program or tool. They ought to be created and maintained for this sole purpose.
All the processes ought to be configured according to the number of users and needs to minimize the work and maximize the use of resources.
We use the first conditional to talk about possible actions in the future.

When we use if in the first conditional, we talk about possible events or actions happening in the future as long as the condition is given.

Structure:

If +present tense sentence + future “will” sentence


Examples:
If she doesn't know the address, will you help her?
If it rains tomorrow, I will stay at home.

We can also use When in conditionals, but it is a little different. It means that the second action is immediately after the first one is complete.
If I don't understand these server processes for next week, I will be in trouble!
When we can use parallelism to create a better performance, reliability in the system will go up.

images.text:
Susan: Jeff, you have to help me out! If I don't understand these server processes for next week, I will be in trouble!
Jeff: Susan, calm down. First of all, do you know what a process in an operating system is?
Susan: It is a mechanism that runs a series of steps. People call this process jobs or tasks, right?
Jeff: Exactly. Now, there are three types of processes: background, user and server processes.
Susan: Well, in a background process, different functions ought to be consolidated, so we don't need many programs to handle and we can monitor other processes. When we use parallelism to create a better performance, reliability in the system will go up.

Jeff: Exactly! User processes are a little different. Their main function is to run software code of an application program or tool. They ought to be created and maintained for this sole purpose.
Susan: Okay. But they can use separate machines for background and user processes, can't they?
Jeff: That's right. You are already taking a grasp of these concepts. They also manage the communication with the server processes through the interface of different programs.
Susan: But then, what do the server processes do?

Jeff: They act as a bridge between the background and user processes; they handle the request and interact with the database. All the processes ought to be configured according to the number of users to minimize the work and maximize the use of resources.
Susan: Okay, I get it now. Last question, what's the purpose of instance memory structures?
Jeff: They store the program code, the shared data, even the private data. Their main objective is to contain and control all the data in the database. Sometimes, these memory structures are internally created for the exclusive use of the processes so users can't even see them.
